domanda: A colleague asks you to document the durability target that Microsoft publishes for locally redundant storage (LRS). Over a given year, what is the minimum durability of objects that LRS is designed to provide?
spiegazione: Correct: LRS replicates data within a single physical datacenter in the primary region and is designed to provide at least 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability of objects over a given year. Why the others are wrong: 'At least 99.9%' is an availability figure for read/write requests, not a durability figure - it is the availability SLA target for hot-tier data, so it is a classic confusion between the availability and durability columns of the redundancy summary table. '12 nines' (99.9999999999%) is the durability target for zone-redundant storage (ZRS), which replicates synchronously across three or more availability zones and therefore earns a higher target than LRS. '16 nines' (99.99999999999999%) is the durability target for the geo-redundant options GRS/RA-GRS and GZRS/RA-GZRS, which add asynchronous replication to a secondary region hundreds of miles away.

domanda: While scripting the deployment of a new Azure Storage account, you must generate a name that Azure will accept. Which naming requirement must the generated name satisfy?
opzione_a: Between 3 and 24 characters, containing only lowercase letters and numbers, and unique across all of Azure
opzione_b: Between 3 and 63 characters, containing lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, and unique within the resource group
opzione_c: Between 1 and 80 characters, containing letters, numbers, hyphens, and underscores, and unique within the subscription
opzione_d: Between 5 and 50 characters, containing only lowercase letters, and unique within the region
spiegazione: Correct: Storage account names must be between 3 and 24 characters in length, can contain only numbers and lowercase letters, and must be unique within Azure. Global uniqueness is required because the account name becomes the subdomain of the public service endpoint, for example https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net. Why the others are wrong: '3 to 63 characters with hyphens, unique within the resource group' describes blob container naming rules (containers do allow hyphens and are scoped to the account), not storage account naming - hyphens are never valid in a storage account name. '1 to 80 characters with hyphens and underscores, unique within the subscription' is close to the generic Azure resource-group naming rule and wrongly scopes uniqueness to the subscription. '5 to 50 characters, unique within the region' invents a limit that does not exist; regional uniqueness would be insufficient because the DNS namespace is global.

domanda: An engineering team needs a storage account that can host both Server Message Block (SMB) and Network File System (NFS) file shares for a latency-sensitive application. Which type of storage account should you create?
spiegazione: Correct: The premium file shares account type is the premium storage account type for Azure Files only, and Microsoft explicitly directs you to it when you want a storage account that supports both SMB and NFS file shares. It is recommended for enterprise or high-performance scale applications and uses SSDs for low latency and high throughput. Why the others are wrong: Standard general-purpose v2 does support Azure Files, but the account overview states that if you want support for NFS in Azure Files you must use the premium file shares account type - so it fails the NFS requirement. Premium block blobs supports only Blob Storage (block blobs and append blobs); it hosts no file shares at all and is aimed at high transaction rates and small objects. Premium page blobs supports page blobs only, which back disk-style workloads rather than SMB or NFS file shares.

domanda: A trading platform stores small objects in a premium block blob storage account to obtain consistently low write latency. The risk team now requires that the data also be replicated to a second, geographically distant region. What should you tell the risk team?
opzione_a: Enable RA-GRS on the existing account from the Redundancy blade in the Azure portal
opzione_b: Premium block blob accounts support only LRS and ZRS, so geo-redundancy cannot be configured on this account type
opzione_c: Open a support request so that Microsoft can perform a support-initiated conversion of the account to GZRS
opzione_d: Convert the account to GZRS by running Start-AzStorageAccountMigration with the -TargetSku parameter
spiegazione: Correct: The premium block blobs account type supports only LRS and ZRS. Geo-redundant options (GRS, RA-GRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS) are not available for this account type, which is why the disaster recovery documentation also states that storage accounts supporting premium block blobs don't currently support geo-redundancy and cannot be failed over. Meeting the requirement means copying data to a separate account in another region, not changing the SKU. Why the others are wrong: Enabling RA-GRS from the Redundancy blade works for standard general-purpose v2 accounts, but the geo-redundant SKUs are simply not offered for premium block blob accounts. A support-initiated conversion cannot create a redundancy option that the account type does not support - and the migration guidance shows premium block blob accounts as supporting neither portal-based nor support-request conversions, only manual migration. Start-AzStorageAccountMigration performs a zone-redundancy conversion (for example LRS to ZRS) on supported account types; it cannot add geo-redundancy, and premium block blob accounts do not support conversion at all.

domanda: Your organization still runs a standard general-purpose v1 storage account in a region that supports availability zones. You must reconfigure the account to use zone-redundant storage (ZRS) while keeping the same account and data. What must you do first?
opzione_a: Upgrade the account to general-purpose v2
opzione_b: Migrate the account from the classic deployment model to Azure Resource Manager
opzione_c: Enable the hierarchical namespace on the account
opzione_d: Change the account's performance tier from Standard to Premium
spiegazione: Correct: General-purpose v1 accounts support only LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS. The migration guidance states that if your storage account is v1, you need to upgrade it to v2 before performing a conversion. A GPv1 account can be upgraded in place to GPv2 with no downtime and no need to copy data, after which the ZRS conversion becomes available. Note the upgrade cannot be undone. Why the others are wrong: Migrating from classic (ASM) to Azure Resource Manager is a real prerequisite for other operations such as customer-managed failover, but the account in this scenario is already a Resource Manager general-purpose v1 account; classic accounts were retired on August 31, 2024. Enabling the hierarchical namespace is a Data Lake Storage capability that has nothing to do with redundancy eligibility - HNS-enabled accounts support the same redundancy options, they merely experience a brief pause of under 30 seconds during a conversion. Changing the performance tier from Standard to Premium is not possible on an existing account, and premium tiers would not be a prerequisite for ZRS in any case.

domanda: A standard general-purpose v2 storage account named contosodata is currently configured for locally redundant storage (LRS) in a region that supports availability zones and has a paired region. You must reconfigure the account for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) without copying the data to a new account. Which approach works?
opzione_a: Set the redundancy directly to GZRS in a single operation on the Redundancy blade
opzione_b: Convert LRS to GRS, and then convert GRS to GZRS
opzione_c: Convert LRS to RA-GRS, and then convert RA-GRS to ZRS
opzione_d: Fail the account over to the secondary region, and then set the redundancy to GZRS
spiegazione: Correct: A direct LRS to GZRS conversion isn't supported. The change requires a two-step process, which can be completed either as LRS to ZRS followed by ZRS to GZRS, or as LRS to GRS followed by GRS to GZRS. Adding geo-redundancy (LRS to GRS) is done with the portal, PowerShell, or the CLI, and adding zone-redundancy (GRS to GZRS) is a conversion; both steps preserve the account and its data. Why the others are wrong: Setting GZRS in a single operation fails because any change that involves zone-redundancy requires a conversion and must be performed separately from the geo-redundancy change - the two aspects cannot be altered in one operation. Converting LRS to RA-GRS and then RA-GRS to ZRS ends at ZRS, which has no geo-redundancy at all, so it does not meet the requirement. Account failover is a disaster recovery mechanism, not a migration tool; it requires an account that is already geo-redundant, and an unplanned failover would actually leave the account as LRS in the new primary region.

domanda: Following a prolonged outage, an administrator initiated a customer-managed (unplanned) failover of a general-purpose v2 storage account that had been configured for GRS. The failover completed successfully. Management now wants the account protected against the loss of a single availability zone in the new primary region. What must you do?
opzione_a: Perform a manual migration of the data to a new zone-redundant storage account
opzione_b: Initiate a customer-initiated conversion from LRS to ZRS on the existing account
opzione_c: Re-enable GRS on the account, and then convert it to GZRS
opzione_d: Fail the account back to the original primary region, and then convert it to GZRS
spiegazione: Correct: A customer-managed unplanned failover automatically converts the storage account to locally redundant storage (LRS) in the new primary region. Microsoft explicitly states that conversion to ZRS or GZRS for an LRS account resulting from a failover isn't supported, and that you must instead perform a manual migration to add zone-redundancy. A manual migration copies the data to a new account with the desired redundancy using a tool such as AzCopy. Why the others are wrong: Initiating an LRS to ZRS conversion is exactly the blocked operation - the FAQ also lists 'account is failed over' as a conflicting scenario for zonal conversions. Re-enabling GRS and then converting to GZRS still requires the zonal conversion step, which remains unsupported on an account that reached LRS through a failover; re-enabling geo-redundancy only restores the geo aspect. Failing back to the original primary region does not help either, because after an unplanned failover the copy of the data in the original primary region is deleted and geo-redundancy is lost; the failed-over account remains ineligible for a zonal conversion.

domanda: A general-purpose v2 storage account is configured for read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) and contains several thousand blobs in the archive tier. A new resiliency standard requires the account to be reconfigured for read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS). You want to keep the existing account. What must you do before the conversion can succeed?
opzione_a: Rehydrate all archived blobs to an online tier
opzione_b: Change the account's default access tier to Cool
opzione_c: Disable soft delete for blobs on the account
opzione_d: Enable the change feed on the account
spiegazione: Correct: The archive tier is supported only for LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS accounts - it isn't supported for ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS accounts. To change the redundancy configuration of an account that contains archived blobs to a zone-redundant option, you must first rehydrate all archived blobs to the hot, cool, or cold tier. The FAQ likewise lists archive data as a conflicting scenario that generates errors during a zonal conversion. Why the others are wrong: Changing the default access tier to Cool only sets the tier inferred by newly uploaded blobs that have no explicit tier; it does nothing to the blobs already sitting in the archive tier, which are the actual blocker. Disabling blob soft delete is unrelated to redundancy conversions - soft delete is a data protection feature and is not listed among the conflicting features for zonal conversions. Enabling the change feed makes matters worse rather than better: the FAQ lists object replication and similar features as conflicting, and change feed is explicitly unsupported for customer-managed planned failover.

domanda: Your change advisory board asks what the impact of a redundancy conversion will be on a general-purpose v2 storage account. Which three statements accurately describe a conversion? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: No data is lost during the conversion, and there is no loss of durability
opzione_b: Access keys, shared access signatures, and service endpoints remain unchanged
opzione_c: The storage account must be re-created in a different region to complete the conversion
opzione_d: An account with a hierarchical namespace enabled might experience a pause of less than 30 seconds
opzione_e: Client applications must be reconfigured to use new service endpoints after the conversion
spiegazione: Correct answers: During a conversion you can access data in your storage account with no loss of durability and no data is lost, and the Azure Storage SLA is maintained throughout. Service endpoints, access keys, shared access signatures, and other account options remain unchanged after the migration. Accounts without a hierarchical namespace experience no interruption to availability, while HNS-enabled accounts might experience a brief pause lasting less than 30 seconds, after which requests complete automatically. Why the others are wrong: Re-creating the account in a different region describes a manual migration, which is the alternative you choose when a conversion isn't supported or when you need to move regions - a conversion operates in place on the existing account. Reconfiguring clients to use new endpoints is unnecessary precisely because the endpoints do not change; that step would be required only after a manual migration to a new account name.

domanda: You are standardizing on zone-redundant storage (ZRS) wherever the account type allows it. Which three storage account types support ZRS? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
spiegazione: Correct answers: The storage account overview lists ZRS as a supported redundancy option for standard general-purpose v2, premium block blobs, and premium file shares. Standard general-purpose v2 is the recommended account type for most scenarios and supports the full range of options (LRS, ZRS, GRS, RA-GRS, GZRS, RA-GZRS); premium block blobs and premium file shares each support LRS and ZRS only, with no geo-redundant options. Note that ZRS availability also varies by region, since the region must support availability zones. Why the others are wrong: Standard general-purpose v1 is a legacy account type that supports only LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS; the redundancy summary lists it under 'Legacy' for LRS and GRS/RA-GRS and shows N/A for ZRS and GZRS. A GPv1 account must be upgraded to GPv2 before a ZRS conversion is possible. Legacy Blob Storage (BlobStorage) accounts likewise support only LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS, and Microsoft recommends upgrading them to general-purpose v2.

domanda: You are reviewing several pending redundancy changes and must identify the ones that cannot be handled by a conversion and therefore require a manual migration. Which three scenarios require a manual migration? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Moving a storage account and its data to a different Azure region
opzione_b: Changing the redundancy of a premium block blob storage account
opzione_c: Changing a standard general-purpose v2 account from LRS to GRS
opzione_d: Adding zone-redundancy to an account that became LRS as the result of a customer-managed unplanned failover
opzione_e: Changing a standard general-purpose v2 account from GRS to GZRS
spiegazione: Correct answers: Microsoft states you must perform a manual migration if you want to migrate your storage account to a different region, or if your storage account is a block blob account - the migration support table confirms premium block blob accounts support neither portal-based nor support-request conversions, only manual migration. Separately, conversion to ZRS or GZRS for an LRS account resulting from a failover isn't supported, and the documentation directs you to perform a manual migration to add zone-redundancy instead. Why the others are wrong: Changing a standard general-purpose v2 account from LRS to GRS is a geo change that you make directly with the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell (Set-AzStorageAccount -SkuName), or the Azure CLI (az storage account update --sku); no manual migration is involved. Changing a general-purpose v2 account from GRS to GZRS is a zone-redundancy conversion, listed in the FAQ among supported zonal conversions and performed as a single conversion on the existing account.

domanda: You are preparing a reference card that summarizes the durability targets Microsoft publishes for Azure Storage redundancy options, together with how many availability zones zone-redundant storage uses. Select the correct value for each item.
opzione_a: Durability of objects over a given year for LRS: [at least 99.9% | at least 99.999999999% (11 nines) | at least 99.99999999999999% (16 nines)]
opzione_b: Durability of objects over a given year for ZRS: [11 nines | 12 nines | 16 nines]
opzione_c: Durability of objects over a given year for GZRS: [11 nines | 12 nines | 16 nines]
opzione_d: Number of availability zones across which ZRS replicates data in the primary region: [two | three or more | six]
risposta_corretta: at least 99.999999999% (11 nines),12 nines,16 nines,three or more
spiegazione: Correct selections: LRS replicates data within a single physical datacenter in the primary region and provides at least 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability of objects over a given year. ZRS copies data synchronously across three or more Azure availability zones in the primary region and offers durability of at least 99.9999999999% (12 nines). GZRS combines ZRS in the primary region with asynchronous replication to a secondary region and is designed to provide at least 99.99999999999999% (16 nines) durability - the same target as GRS, because within the secondary region data is always replicated synchronously using LRS. Why the other choices are wrong: 'At least 99.9%' is the availability target for read and write requests, not a durability figure, and is a common confusion between the availability and durability rows of the redundancy summary table. Assigning 11 or 12 nines to GZRS understates it by ignoring the secondary region, while assigning 16 nines to ZRS overstates it, since ZRS alone does not protect against a regional disaster. 'Two' zones is wrong because a ZRS write returns successfully only after data is written to all replicas across the three availability zones; 'six' is not a documented figure.

domanda: A media company is designing storage for an application that requires enterprise-grade Azure file shares over both SMB and NFS, consistently low latency, and resilience to the loss of a single availability zone within the primary region. Select the correct option for each item.
opzione_a: Storage account type to create: [Standard general-purpose v2 | Premium block blobs | Premium file shares]
opzione_b: Performance tier of this account type: [Standard | Premium]
opzione_c: Most resilient redundancy option supported by this account type: [ZRS | GZRS | RA-GZRS]
opzione_d: Read access to a secondary region for Azure Files: [Supported | Not supported]
spiegazione: Correct selections: The premium file shares account type is the premium storage account type for file shares only and is the type Microsoft names when you need a storage account that supports both SMB and NFS file shares. It is a premium performance account, and premium performance storage accounts use solid-state drives (SSDs) to deliver low latency and high throughput. Premium file shares support LRS and ZRS only, so ZRS is the most resilient option available and it satisfies the requirement to survive the loss of one availability zone - Microsoft also recommends ZRS for Azure Files because no remounting of shares is required if a zone becomes unavailable. Finally, Azure Files doesn't support read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS) or read-access geo-zone-redundant storage (RA-GZRS). Why the other choices are wrong: Standard general-purpose v2 supports Azure Files but not NFS shares, and Premium block blobs hosts no file shares at all. Selecting Standard for the performance tier contradicts both the account type and the low-latency requirement. GZRS and RA-GZRS are not offered for premium file share accounts, which have no geo-redundant options.

domanda: The account fin-prod is a standard general-purpose v2 storage account configured for LRS. It resides in a region that supports availability zones and has a paired region, contains no archived blobs, and has never been failed over. You must reconfigure it for RA-GZRS using the fewest possible redundancy change operations, without copying data to a new account. Select the correct option for each item.
opzione_a: Minimum number of redundancy change operations required: [one | two | three]
opzione_b: First operation: [LRS to RA-GRS | LRS to RA-GZRS | LRS to GZRS]
opzione_c: Second operation: [RA-GRS to RA-GZRS | RA-GRS to ZRS | none required]
opzione_d: Minimum time you must wait after a zone-redundancy conversion before changing the redundancy setting again: [24 hours | 72 hours | 7 days]
risposta_corretta: two,LRS to RA-GRS,RA-GRS to RA-GZRS,72 hours
spiegazione: Correct selections: Geo-redundancy and read-access can be changed together, but any change that also involves zone-redundancy requires a conversion and must be performed separately, so two operations are the minimum. The first operation switches LRS to RA-GRS using the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, or the Azure CLI - the migration table shows this as a direct change from LRS to GRS/RA-GRS. The second operation is the zone-redundancy conversion RA-GRS to RA-GZRS, which the FAQ lists explicitly among supported zonal conversions. After a zone-redundancy conversion you must wait at least 72 hours before changing the redundancy setting of the account again, so that background processes can complete and account consistency and integrity are preserved. Why the other choices are wrong: 'One' operation is impossible because a direct LRS to GZRS conversion isn't supported, and 'three' is more than the minimum. Choosing 'LRS to RA-GZRS' or 'LRS to GZRS' as the first step repeats that unsupported single-hop change. 'RA-GRS to ZRS' would strip the geo-redundancy the first step just added, and 'none required' contradicts the two-step requirement. '24 hours' and '7 days' are not the documented interval.

domanda:
The account sales-gpv2 is a standard general-purpose v2 storage account configured for locally redundant storage (LRS). It is located in a region that supports availability zones and has a paired region. The account contains no blobs in the archive tier, does not have NFSv3 enabled, and has never been failed over. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. You can change the account from LRS to GRS by using the Azure portal.
2. You can change the account from LRS to GZRS in a single operation by using the Azure portal.
3. You can change the account from LRS to ZRS by initiating a customer-initiated conversion.
opzione_a: You can change the account from LRS to GRS by using the Azure portal.
opzione_b: You can change the account from LRS to GZRS in a single operation by using the Azure portal.
opzione_c: You can change the account from LRS to ZRS by initiating a customer-initiated conversion.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: Adding geo-redundancy is a change you make directly with the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, or the Azure CLI. The migration table shows LRS to GRS/RA-GRS as a direct change on the Redundancy blade under Data management. Note that adding geo-redundancy incurs a one-time egress charge because the entire account is replicated to the secondary region. Statement 2 - No: A direct LRS to GZRS conversion isn't supported. Any change that involves zone-redundancy requires a conversion and must be performed separately from the geo-redundancy change, so the account must go through a two-step process - either LRS to ZRS then ZRS to GZRS, or LRS to GRS then GRS to GZRS. Statement 3 - Yes: Adding zone-redundancy to a standard general-purpose v2 account is a conversion, and customers in most regions can start a customer-initiated conversion and monitor its progress from the Azure portal, with Azure PowerShell (Start-AzStorageAccountMigration -TargetSku), or with the Azure CLI (az storage account migration start). Microsoft recommends customer-initiated conversion over a support-initiated conversion whenever possible. The scenario rules out the usual blockers, such as archived blobs, NFSv3, and a prior failover.

domanda:
An application team owns a standard general-purpose v2 storage account named webassets that is configured for read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS). The account stores block blobs. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. After a customer-managed (unplanned) failover completes, the account is automatically configured as RA-GRS in the new primary region.
2. The secondary read endpoint for Blob Storage is https://webassets-secondary.blob.core.windows.net.
3. Blobs in this account can be moved to the archive tier.
opzione_a: After a customer-managed (unplanned) failover completes, the account is automatically configured as RA-GRS in the new primary region.
opzione_b: The secondary read endpoint for Blob Storage is https://webassets-secondary.blob.core.windows.net.
opzione_c: Blobs in this account can be moved to the archive tier.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: Initiating a customer-managed unplanned failover automatically converts the storage account to locally redundant storage (LRS) in the new primary region and deletes the storage account in the original primary region, so geo-redundancy is lost rather than retained. You can re-enable GRS or RA-GRS afterward, but re-replicating the data to the new secondary region incurs a charge. This is the key contrast with a customer-managed planned failover, after which geo-redundancy is retained and the account is converted to GRS. Statement 2 - Yes: When read access to the secondary is enabled, the secondary endpoint appends the suffix -secondary to the account name. If the primary blob endpoint is webassets.blob.core.windows.net, the secondary endpoint is webassets-secondary.blob.core.windows.net, and the account access keys are the same for both endpoints. Statement 3 - Yes: Only storage accounts configured for LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS support moving blobs to the archive tier. Because this account is RA-GRS, archiving is supported; it would not be supported if the account were ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS.

domanda: The account archivedata is a standard general-purpose v2 storage account configured for locally redundant storage (LRS). It contains blobs in the archive tier. You must reconfigure the account for geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS) by adding zone-redundancy first, without copying the data to a new storage account. Arrange the required actions in the correct order.
opzione_a: Rehydrate all blobs in the archive tier to an online tier
opzione_b: Perform a conversion from ZRS to GZRS
opzione_c: Wait at least 72 hours for background processes to complete
opzione_d: Initiate a customer-initiated conversion from LRS to ZRS
opzione_e: Verify that the storage account's region supports zone-redundant storage
spiegazione: Correct order: (1) Verify that the account's region supports zone-redundant storage - Microsoft directs you to make sure the region where your storage account is located supports all of the desired replication settings before converting, and attempting a zonal conversion in an unsupported region generates an error. (2) Rehydrate all archived blobs to an online tier, because the archive tier isn't supported for ZRS, GZRS, or RA-GZRS accounts; to convert an LRS, GRS, or RA-GRS account to a zone-redundant option you must first move archived blobs to the hot, cool, or cold tier. (3) Initiate the customer-initiated conversion from LRS to ZRS, which adds zone-redundancy and can be started from the Azure portal, Azure PowerShell, or the Azure CLI. (4) Wait at least 72 hours, because after a zone-redundancy conversion you must wait that long before changing the redundancy setting of the account again so background processes can complete. (5) Perform the ZRS to GZRS change, which adds geo-redundancy and completes the two-step path. This ordering matters: verification precedes work, the archive blocker must clear before any zonal conversion is attempted, and the mandatory 72-hour hold falls between the two redundancy changes, not before them.
